utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were there strong armed resistance, was there a strong armed resistance in Prusac village?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were ready to fight. However, they didn't have enough weapons or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We know from your statement that you left Donji Vakuf in May. You left for Bugojno and joined the army, and you were also able to observe some of these military operations. What I'm interested, and it is one of my last questions, is were there any mosques in Prusac, in the Prusac village?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in 1992, which conditions they -- in which condition they were -- we could find these mosques in the village of Prusac?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, which means the August and September of 1992, these mosques were riddled with bullets of different calibres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were you able to see whether, if the mosques had minaret, whether it was destroyed or whether they were still standing?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a part of them were destroyed. However, the minaret was still standing on the central mosque in Prusac, and the condition of the other mosques was similar but I must say I don't remember that the mosque in Rijeka, in the new settlement as we called it, had a minaret at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know how many mosques or how many Muslim religious properties were in Prusac?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were four mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we'll go back to Prusac village, we already heard that it was a Muslim village. This resistance in Prusac, for how long did it last and what was the result of all the actions against the village of Prusac?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. You mean only this period, when the Serb units attacked?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What I'm referring, I want to start on 17 and whether the actions went beyond the 17 of August.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After this action, after this operation, there was only fierce artillery fire, shelling of houses, and of the army positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after the 17th, were there other military actions against Prusac?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of this kind. Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did the Muslim population of the village of Prusac stayed in the village throughout the war or did they move?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of them remained in Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the rest?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I said a part of the population stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened to the rest of the population? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Children, the elderly, a part of the women, left for Bugojno, and many found shelter in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. This concludes my examination-in-chief, and I'm sorry it took longer than I anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Mr. Ackerman? I wish to make it clear that we need to stop at 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think it's unlikely that I will conclude by 6.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I said what I said precisely because I do not expect you will finish by 6.30 so I hope the witness has been informed that he may have to stay the weekend here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At some point I would like at least a ten minute break, between now and 6.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends whether you would like it now, before you start your cross, or whether you would like it at some later point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we did it now that would leave us with about 45 minutes -- 40 minutes left to go, and I think that would be appropriate and it would also be a relief to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will stop for 10 minutes. We will have a break of 10 minutes. At least 15 minutes you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 10 is fine with me. Whatever is good for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have a break of 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, by the way, sir, is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, we will get started and get as far as we can before 6.30. I want you to have, to look at, the statements you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in September of 2001. If you go to the first page of your statement, I think it's the third paragraph, beginning with the language, "All ethnic groups in Donji Vakuf," you'll find a sentence in there that reads as follows: "Very often in this period, the SDS representatives from Donji Vakuf - I can't specifically say who - assembled volunteers who went to Banja Luka for military training." Do I take it from that that you have no idea who SDS representatives involved in this claim you make were?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who rallied these people and who specifically was in charge of the sending of volunteers for training to Banja Luka but I know the people who went for their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is that the source of your information, that you know people who went for that training?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What kind of a military training facility was in Banja Luka that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know an officer who went for a training course for logistical support. I also know a member of the army who went for the so-called special training, training for special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that they could not have gone to Banja Luka based on their assignment in the reserve forces. The two of them were assigned to serve in the Territorial Defence units in the municipality of Donji Vakuf and I did not send them to their training. Somebody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you said one of them went to training for special units. What would that be? What kind of training is that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that term, "Special units," I understand the reconnaissance and sabotage units, the kind that we also had in our force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, that kind of training was offered in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Had you ever sent anybody from your TO to Banja Luka for sabotage special unit training?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, because organisationally speaking, I wasn't linked with Banja Luka. I was linked with Zenica. Donji Vakuf was in the Zenica district.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you really aren't familiar with what kind of training might have been available in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew that all available training could have been completed in Zenica because the district staff of Zenica and the district staff of Banja Luka provided similar kinds of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the answer is that you don't know what kind of training might have been available in Banja Luka? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that any course of training that was available in Banja Luka was available in Zenica too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So far you've indicated that you know of two people who went to Banja Luka for training, one for logistics and one for special unit training. Is that all you know about?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other men whose names I don't know, they were younger men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What basis do you have for concluding that SDS representatives had anything to do with this?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I talked to a man who went to Banja Luka for their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you learned that from one person who went to Banja Luka? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was no secret. Many people knew about that fact and about that activity. I was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And isn't it the case, as you have suggested, that none of this involved combat training but either special unit, logistics, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the kind of training we provided in Donji Vakuf as well, on the level of the municipal TO staff, as well as in the district staff of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is the answer to my question yes?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it the case, as you have suggested, that none of this involved combat training but either special unit, logistics, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that, don't you, that there was no place in Banja Luka where one could receive combat training? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the drill grounds in Manjaca, near Banja Luka, combat training was also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but you didn't say they went to Manjaca. You said they went to Banja Luka, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said they went to Banja Luka, I implied the environs of Banja Luka as well. Any municipality in the vicinity of Banja Luka as well. However, they said they were going to Banja Luka and that included Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's now your position that Banja Luka, the way you said it in your statement, could have included Banja Luka municipality and any municipality bordering Banja Luka? Is that what you're telling us now?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know where exactly they went. All I know is that they went to Banja Luka, because that's the way they put it, but where specifically they received their training in that barracks or outside Banja Luka or at Manjaca, or in a settlement near Banja Luka, they didn't explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go down about a paragraph and a half, there is a paragraph that begins and continues with this language: "At the beginning of 1992, citizens in Donji Vakuf were hearing detonations coming from the direction of Kupres and bursts of gunfire in town during the night." Do you know what was happening in Kupres in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that there were -- there was fighting in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at some documents? I'd like you to look first at P1713. The document you have before you, sir, comes from the 30th Partisan Division command. It is signed at the end by Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Kokovic, and I just need to go through it with you. It says, "On 13 April, 1992, a meeting was held with representatives of the municipal authorities of Donji Vakuf and Bugojno, with the aim of coordinating views and tasks in order to maintain the peace in this region. Donji Vakuf municipality was represented by the President of the municipal assembly, Bugojno municipality was represented by the President and vice-president of the municipal assembly, and the commander of the Territorial Defence staff." My first question is: Did you attend this meting?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. But I heard about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it indicates that the meeting was chaired by Colonel Galic, and then indicates what he said, opening the meeting. And if you go down just a little ways through this, he is speaking of the tasks of the JNA and says this: "Their task is to ensure peace, prevent interethnic clashes, put all military formations under our command and prevent the activities of all paramilitary formations." Do you see that? Find where I'm reading from? It's actually the second paragraph of his remarks.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, he says that it's one of his tasks to put all military formations under the command of the JNA and prevent the activities of all paramilitary formations. Now, you spoke earlier today about the creation of a brigade that was put under the command of the JNA, that was created from former paramilitary formations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He goes on to say that "The situation at Kupres was intolerable, there were several armies and paramilitary formations there and they all sowed fear and terror." If we go on down a couple of paragraphs, he then says, "I appeal to you," talking primarily to the Presidents of these two municipalities, Donji Vakuf and Bugojno, "I appeal to you to be sincere and concise during the discussion. And not like it was at Kupres. Then we reached a full agreement and talked until 2400 hours on 2 April, 1992, when HOS, Croatian defence forces, had already been dispatched and attacked innocent people. The members of the HOS were originally from all areas except this and when the attack had begun, we called for a cease-fire several times but to no avail." Now, are you familiar with the attack in the Kupres area by the Croatian Defence forces?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about the fighting, but as far as HOS is concerned, the Croatian Defence forces, attacking Serb forces, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in 14 -- on 13 April, 1992, who was the President of the Donji Vakuf municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Kemal Terzic in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look on the next page, Kemal Terzic made some observations, Kemal Terzic was Bosniak, correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Kemal Terzic said, "We have not had a single interethnic clash in Donji Vakuf. We have not had a single case of looting." A little further down, he says, "85 per cent of Serbian families have moved out, to Novi Sad, Banja Luka, Belgrade, 95 per cent of Muslim families are here in town." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the Bosniak Kemal Terzic was incorrect when he said those things on that day? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he could have said this, because it's absolutely impossible that he should have stated this on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to -- it's page 3 in the English version, it's Colonel Galic speaking after the vice-president of Bugojno, Misic, speaks. And Galic makes a request of Sojic, you know who Sojic is? Is he the municipal -- yeah, it's probably Sajic, the municipal president of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soljic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, is he the municipal president from Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: According to this, Galic asks him, "Are there any paramilitary formations in the Bugojno area" and he replies as follows: "Everyone is armed. That is a fact and everyone knows that. I guarantee there is no one from outside." Galic then asks, "What would happen if we went to Kupres via Bugojno?" His reply was, "We cannot give you any guarantees on that." Do you know why he couldn't guarantee safe passage for the military to go through Bugojno on the way to Kupres?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next person who speaks is Colonel Selak, who you know to be the head of the logistics base in Banja Luka and a Bosniak serving in the JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Colonel Selak?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't introduced to him but I was once at the warehouse in Daljan, near him, standing near him literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Selak says, "Cooperation has been exceptionally good so far. There are extremists on all sides but they can be very dangerous if they come from the outside and provoke incidents." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not correct what he said or it's not correct that I read it correctly? It's what the document says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct for this reason: It's not true that cooperation had been exceptionally good that far. Cooperation wasn't good because all the agreements that had been reached were breached. Second, he says that there are extremists on all sides and they are especially dangerous if they are coming from outside and provoking incidents. Why did officers from Banja Luka come then? And I would like to know who was it who came from outside and who were the extremists on the Muslim side in Donji Vakuf. I don't know any such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a meeting that you did not attend, correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And yet you presume to sit here in front of these Judges and tell them that you know for sure that Osman Selak said nothing of the kind. Is that your position? Even though you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. What I mean is that it's possible he said that, but I'm saying that his claims are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Then finally, Colonel Galic wants to try to adopt some conclusions as a result of this meeting that has gone on, and I'd like to refer to a few of them. Number 3, is efforts should be made to set up mixed police checkpoints and that checkpoints be manned by personnel of all ethnic backgrounds. Now that came to pass, did it not? That's exactly what happened, right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mixed police checkpoints never existed in Donji Vakuf, not in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 5 says, ensure unobstructed travel along the Banja Luka-Jajce-Donji Vakuf-Bugojno-Kupres road and the Bugojno-Travnik road. In this regard the tunnel at Kupreska Vrata should be cleared of mines. Where is that tunnel at Kupreska Vrata in proximity to Kupres itself? How close is it to Kupres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it can be indicated on the map where he has already indicated the two -- the bridge and the other, I think it would --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not on the map, Your Honour, Kupres is off that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's off that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's two kilometres away from Kupres in the direction of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the tunnel being mined?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then number 9, Colonel Galic says that they should prevent further departures from the municipalities and take measures to encourage those who have moved away to return. Do you know if that was ever done?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like to you look at another document, DB120, please. DB120, sir is a document from the 5th Corps command, 11 April, 1992. First thing I want you to look at is the last page. And on the last page I think you will see that it is signed by Colonel Mesud Hasotic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Colonel Mesud Hasotic was a Bosniak serving in the JNA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't Mesud a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He says, in this report, of 11 April, 1992, "In several crisis areas in BH, there is an escalation of open conflicts of ever-increasing intensity with tragic consequences in terms of human life and property. The situation is most critical in Kupres, Bijeljina, Bosanski Brod, Sarajevo and Foca. According to some of the evidence received up to 9 April, several hundred people have been killed there, mostly women and children. The most serious suffering is being experienced by the people of Kupres where heavy fighting is taking place between the armed formations of Croatia and the Serbian people from these parts. The objective of the Croatian state's diabolical plans is to take Kupres regardless of casualties and to join up the BH, HDZ, that's the Croatian Democratic Union paramilitaries, along the Bugojno, Doboj, Bosanski Brod axis. This would effectively sever the Serbian Krajinas from the remainder of Yugoslavia. In all the larger towns along the above-mentioned axis, HOS, Croatian defence forces, and ZNG, National Guard Corps units have taken and are firmly holding on to key positions. They are controlling whatever traffic there is, capturing, harassing and abusing primarily Serbs and JNA members. An unprecedented crime was committed in Kupres, 28 people were slaughtered." Now, you know, don't you, that that was true, that that was the mission of the Croatian forces, exactly as described in this report by Colonel Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were -- spent part of this time very nearby in Kupres -- I mean in Donji Vakuf, and another part of this time in 1992 as a member of the military in Bugojno and you don't know what was going on in Kupres, which was a few kilometres away from you? You want to tell the Court you don't know what know what was going on over there?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on during this fighting, in this period, around the 11th of April, or generally in April, because I was in Donji Vakuf and I was hiding, going from house to house, because I didn't dare to sleep in my own house for fear of being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think we need to stop at that point because the next document is fairly detailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman, and thank you, Mr. Alkic. I'm afraid, as you see, we haven't managed to finish today. It's nobody's fault. It's just happens that you are a key witness in this municipality and a lot of information obviously is needed from you, from both the Prosecution and the Defence, and therefore I ask you to be patient. We'll meet Monday in the afternoon. All sittings next week are in the afternoon, even though I am trying to find out whether we could find a courtroom any of those five days in the morning but I don't promise as yet, I don't think it's going to be easy but I'm trying. It will be in Trial Chamber III, courtroom III, sorry, courtroom III. In the meantime, the usher can escort the witness out. Have a nice weekend, sir, and we'll meet on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova? We need to finish --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is very short, I only want to confirm that on Monday, we will hear the witness 7.136, and if we are talking about exhibits, I would like to ask you to bring the Prnjavor binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And on Wednesday, we are calling Witness 7.265, and your legal officer got all the statements, transcripts, which are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. On Wednesday, I have two Status Conferences as well in the morning. So thank you. Have a nice weekend, we'll meet on -- meet Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm hoping for a better week next week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
